report.source_text: Contrast-enhanced MRI (CE-MRI) showed a large infiltrative lesion involving left hemicalvarium, a dural-based T1 isointense, T2 hypointense enhancing mass (with predominantly extraparenchymal and minimal intraparenchymal component) along left temporal lobe along with extensive pachy-meningeal thickening along the left cerebral hemisphere and cervical spinal canal. Significant perilesional oedema was seen in left temporal lobe. Mass was contiguously invading left transverse and sigmoid sinus. Mass also showed retropharyngeal spread up to the superior mediastinum with cervical and upper dorsal vertebral body involvement. ‘Dot-in-circle’ sign was seen on MRI in the cervical soft tissues, which is typical of soft-tissue mycetomas (figure 3).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A male teenager presented with a 7-year history of slowly progressive asymptomatic swelling over the nape of the neck that gradually extended to cover the entire neck and adjacent scalp. The swelling was characterized by multiple elevated lesions with intermittent discharge of reddish-yellow fluid, associated with difficulty in neck mobility and mouth opening. Physical examination revealed a large (25 cm × 10 cm), firm-to-hard, non-tender, fixed swelling with papules, plaques, brown-colored crusts, and atrophic scars. The patient had poor dental hygiene and a family history of agricultural exposure. Cutaneous punch biopsy demonstrated filamentous gram-positive bacilli with characteristic Splendore-Hoeppli reaction and suppurative granulation tissue, while special stains (GMS, PAS, ZN) were negative, ruling out fungi and mycobacteria. Tissue cultures were negative. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed extensive disease with left hemicalvarium involvement, dural-based mass, pachy-meningeal thickening, retropharyngeal spread to superior mediastinum, cervical and upper dorsal vertebral body involvement, and the characteristic 'dot-in-circle' sign typical of soft-tissue mycetomas. Initial treatment with ceftriaxone and penicillin G resulted in only 20% improvement, followed by disease recurrence. A revised diagnosis of actinomycetoma was made, and second-line therapy with amikacin, rifampicin, and cotrimoxazole was initiated. At 1-month follow-up, the swelling had decreased by 60%, with continued oral penicillin G, doxycycline, metronidazole, and prednisolone.
